question: May a California notary who isn't an attorney give legal advice?

options.why: Correct. Giving legal advice without a law license is the unauthorized practice of law under Business and Professions Code §6125.
Wrong. Advising on what a notarized document should say or do is still legal advice.
Wrong. Free advice is still the unauthorized practice of law.
Wrong. A disclaimer can't authorize something the law prohibits.

explanation: Non-attorney notaries may not give legal advice.
source: Cal. Sec. of State Notary Public Handbook (Acts Constituting the Practice of Law)

refs.title: General Information: Acts Constituting the Practice of Law (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 8)

question: Under Government Code §8224, when may a notary NOT perform a notarial act?

options.text: When they have a direct financial or beneficial interest in the transaction
options.why: Correct. Government Code §8224 bars a notary from acting when they have a direct financial or beneficial interest in the transaction.

options.text: When the signer is a stranger
options.why: Wrong. Strangers are the most common signers; there's no rule against notarizing for them.
Wrong. Document length has nothing to do with conflicts of interest.
Wrong. A signer's age isn't a ground to refuse.

explanation: A notary must not notarize where they have a direct financial or beneficial interest.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8224 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 41)
General Information: Conflict of Interest (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 12)

question: May a non-attorney notary advertise using the term 'notario público'?

options.text: No; the literal translation is prohibited
options.why: Correct. §8219.5 prohibits non-attorney notaries from using 'notario público' or similar translations, which suggest legal powers.
Wrong. Spanish-language ads are exactly where the ban applies.
Wrong. A disclaimer doesn't cure the prohibited term.
Wrong. California law governs California commissions, wherever else the notary may be licensed.

explanation: Non-attorney notaries may not use 'notario público' or similar translations in advertising.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8219.5 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 40)

question: A non-attorney notary advertises notary services in a language other than English. What must the ad include?

options.text: A notice, in English and the other language, that the notary is not an attorney and may not give legal advice about immigration or any other legal matter, and the fees
options.why: Correct. §8219.5 requires a notice in English and the other language that the notary isn't an attorney and can't give legal advice about immigration or other legal matters, plus the fees.
Wrong. The notice is mandatory for non-English ads.
Wrong. A home address isn't the required content.
Wrong. Bond details aren't required in ads.

explanation: Non-English ads must include a notice that the notary isn't an attorney and can't give legal advice, plus the fees.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8219.5 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 40)

question: What is the consequence of a first violation of the 'notario' advertising rule?

options.text: Suspension of the commission for at least one year
options.why: Correct. §8219.5 requires a suspension of at least one year for a first violation, and revocation for a second.
Wrong. A first violation brings at least a one-year suspension, not a warning.
Wrong. The statute does impose a penalty.
Wrong. $15 is the notarial fee, not a penalty.

explanation: A first offense results in suspension of at least one year; a second results in revocation.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8219.5 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 40)

question: May a non-attorney notary act as an immigration consultant?

options.text: Only if they are qualified and bonded as an immigration consultant under the Business and Professions Code
options.why: Correct. Under §8223, a non-attorney notary may act as an immigration consultant only if separately qualified and bonded under the Business and Professions Code.
Wrong. Immigration consulting is tightly restricted.
Wrong. Being bilingual isn't a qualification for immigration services.
Wrong. The $15 cap on notarizing forms doesn't authorize consulting.

explanation: A non-attorney notary may not act as an immigration consultant unless separately qualified and bonded.
source: Cal. Gov't Code §8223; Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §22440

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8223 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 41)
General Information: Immigration Documents (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 20)

question: May a notary notarize their own signature?

options.why: Correct. Notarizing one's own signature is the clearest possible direct interest under §8224.
Wrong. The notary can't be impartial about their own signature.
Wrong. A witness doesn't remove the notary's self-interest.
Wrong. Personal documents are exactly the conflict §8224 prohibits.

explanation: Notaries cannot notarize their own signatures.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8224 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 41)

question: Which is a ground for the Secretary of State to deny, suspend or revoke a commission?

options.text: Failure to fully and faithfully discharge the duties of a notary
options.why: Correct. §8214.1 lists failure to fully and faithfully discharge a notary's duties as a ground for discipline.

options.text: Moving within California and reporting it
options.why: Wrong. Moving within California and reporting it on time is compliance.

options.text: Charging less than the maximum fee
options.why: Wrong. Fees are maximums; charging less is allowed.
Wrong. Documents may be notarized in California for use anywhere.

explanation: §8214.1 lists grounds including failure to faithfully discharge duties.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8214.1 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 37)

question: What is the maximum civil penalty for negligently failing to obtain satisfactory evidence of identity?

options.why: Correct. Government Code §8214.15 allows a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for negligently failing to obtain satisfactory evidence.
Wrong. $500 is the address-change penalty.
Wrong. $1,500 is the penalty for failing to secure the journal or seal.
Wrong. $2,500 is the penalty for failing to take a thumbprint.

explanation: Failure to obtain satisfactory evidence can bring a civil penalty of up to $10,000.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1185 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 46)

question: Who is liable for damages caused by a notary's misconduct or neglect?

options.text: The notary, and the surety up to the $15,000 bond
options.why: Correct. Under §8214, the notary is liable for all damages, and the surety is liable up to the $15,000 bond.
Wrong. The surety's liability is capped and it can seek repayment; the notary stays liable.
Wrong. An employer may be liable in some cases, but the notary remains liable.
Wrong. The State doesn't insure notaries.

explanation: Notaries and their sureties are liable for damages from misconduct or neglect.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8214 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 37)
General Information: Notary Public Bond (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 8)

question: A notary knowingly and willfully, with intent to defraud, notarizes a deed of trust on a single-family home that they know is forged. What is it under Government Code §8214.2?

options.why: Correct. §8214.2 makes it a felony to knowingly and willfully, with intent to defraud, perform a notarial act on a deed of trust on a home of up to four units, knowing it is false or forged.
Wrong. §8214.2 makes this a felony.

options.text: Only grounds for a civil penalty
options.why: Wrong. It is a felony, and §8214.2 adds that this is not the only remedy.

options.text: Not an offense if the notary charged no fee
options.why: Wrong. Whether a fee was charged has no bearing; the fraudulent act is the offense.

explanation: Knowingly notarizing a false or forged deed of trust on a single-family residence (up to four units) with intent to defraud is a felony under §8214.2. Other penalties and remedies still apply.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8214.2 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 38)

question: A signer asks the notary to backdate the certificate. The notary should:

options.why: Correct. A backdated certificate states a false date, which is misconduct with civil and criminal exposure.

options.text: Agree if the signer signed earlier
options.why: Wrong. The certificate shows the date of the notarial act, not of signing.
Wrong. A waiver can't legalize a false certificate.
Wrong. Payment doesn't make a false date true, and charging extra is an overcharge.

explanation: Backdating creates a false certificate, which carries civil and criminal penalties.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8214.1 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 37)

question: Must the signer personally appear?

options.why: Correct. Personal appearance before the notary is essential for every traditional notarial act.

options.text: No, a phone call is enough
options.why: Wrong. A phone call isn't appearance and lets an impostor pose as the signer.
Wrong. An employer's assurance doesn't replace the signer's appearance.
Wrong. There's no exception for relatives.

explanation: Signers must personally appear before the notary.
source: Cal. Civ. Code §1189; Cal. Sec. of State Notary Public Handbook

question: Is a notary responsible for the content of a document?

options.text: No; the boxed consumer notice says the notary verifies identity only
options.why: Correct. The boxed consumer notice states that the notary verifies only identity, not the document's truthfulness, accuracy or validity.
Wrong. Reviewing contents isn't the notary's role.
Wrong. No document type makes the notary responsible for its content.
Wrong. Reading a document doesn't make the notary vouch for it.

explanation: The notary verifies identity, not the truth or validity of the document.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1189 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 48)

question: A document has blank spaces. What should the notary do?

options.text: Ask the signer to complete or strike them before notarizing
options.why: Correct. Blanks should be completed or struck through so nothing can be added after notarization.
Wrong. Notarizing with blanks invites fraudulent additions.
Wrong. Notaries must never fill in document content.
Wrong. Initials beside blanks don't stop someone filling them in later.

explanation: Blanks should be completed or struck before notarizing.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8205 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 31)
General Information: Notarization of Incomplete Documents (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 19)

question: A notary is convicted of a felony during the commission. What can happen?

options.text: The Secretary of State may revoke the commission
options.why: Correct. A felony conviction is grounds for revocation under §8214.1 at any point during the commission.
Wrong. The Secretary of State need not wait for renewal.
Wrong. The surety can cancel the bond but not the commission.
Wrong. Revocation is the Secretary of State's power, not the county clerk's.

explanation: A felony conviction is grounds for revocation.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8214.1 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 37)

question: Is it misconduct to fail to complete a certificate at the time the signature is acknowledged?

options.text: Yes; it's a listed ground for discipline
options.why: Correct. §8214.1 lists failure to complete the acknowledgment at the time the signature is acknowledged as a ground for discipline.
Wrong. There is a timing requirement: at the time of the act.
Wrong. The rule applies to all acknowledgments, not just deeds.
Wrong. It's misconduct whether or not anyone complains.

explanation: Failing to complete the acknowledgment at the time of the act is grounds for discipline.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8214.1 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 37)

question: A notary prepares and files immigration documents for a fee while not qualified. Besides discipline, what can result?

options.text: Civil penalties and possible criminal prosecution
options.why: Correct. Unlawful immigration services can bring civil penalties, criminal prosecution and loss of commission.
Wrong. The consequences are serious.
Wrong. Penalties go well beyond refunds.
Wrong. Unlawful immigration services are penalized, not rewarded.

explanation: Unlawful immigration services can lead to civil penalties, prosecution and loss of commission.
source: Cal. Gov't Code §8223; Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §22440

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8223 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 41)

question: May a notary refuse to notarize if the signer can't be identified?

options.why: Correct. Without satisfactory evidence of identity, the notary must refuse; it's the core safeguard.
Wrong. Proceeding without identification violates §1185.
Wrong. No permission is needed to refuse an unlawful notarization.
Wrong. Identification is required for every act.

explanation: A notary must refuse if identity can't be established.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1185 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 46)

question: A notary is related to the signer but has no financial interest. May they notarize?

options.text: California doesn't prohibit it outright, but it's best avoided because impartiality may be questioned
options.why: Correct. §8224 bars direct financial or beneficial interests, not family ties as such, but notarizing for relatives is discouraged because impartiality may be questioned.
Wrong. California has no blanket ban on relatives (Florida bans spouse, parents and children).
Wrong. It's discouraged, not encouraged.
Wrong. No court order is involved.

explanation: California bars notarizing with a direct financial or beneficial interest; notarizing for relatives is discouraged but not expressly banned.
